_sources.usda: USDA FoodData Central, https://fdc.nal.usda.gov/ (record named in each entry), read 2026-10-27
_sources.nihOds: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements fact sheets (Iron, Folate, Vitamin C, Vitamin K, Magnesium, Zinc, Potassium, Vitamin A, Calcium, Vitamin B12, Vitamin D, Vitamin E), https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/list-all/; reference intakes as listed in build_draft_batch.py (RDA for adult women)
_sources.niddk: NIDDK, Eating, Diet & Nutrition for Kidney Stones, read 2026-10-26: nuts and nut products, peanuts, rhubarb, spinach and wheat bran listed among foods to reduce for calcium oxalate stones

burdock.desc: Burdock root, cooked, boiled, drained, without salt
burdock.portion: ½ cup pieces, cooked (USDA: 1 cup of 1 in pieces = 125 g)
burdock.how: Peel or scrub, then slice thin and simmer or stir-fry (kinpira style); it keeps a firm, earthy bite.
burdock.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
burdock.name: Burdock

wakame.how: Soak dried wakame briefly, then add to miso soup or a cucumber salad. This record is raw wakame, so a rehydrated serving is the closer match.
wakame.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
wakame.reviewNote: Raw (as USDA lists it); dried wakame is far more concentrated by weight. Seaweed iodine content is not in a nutrient record here; the existing catalogue caution ("Iodine: normal portions") is carried over without an external source.
wakame.name: Wakame

kelp.how: Add small pieces to soups and grain pots or rehydrate for salads; a little goes a long way.
kelp.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
kelp.reviewNote: Raw kelp. Iodine can exceed the safe limit (existing catalogue cautions: carried over, not externally sourced here; NIH ODS has an iodine fact sheet that has not been read this session).
kelp.name: Kelp

water-chestnut.how: Slice raw or tinned for stir-fries, salads and dumpling fillings, where it stays crisp when cooked.
water-chestnut.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
water-chestnut.name: Water chestnut

parsley.how: Chop into salads, grain dishes, sauces and soups, or stir through at the end of cooking so the flavour stays fresh.
parsley.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
parsley.name: Parsley

rhubarb.portion: ½ cup diced (USDA: 1 cup diced = 122 g)
rhubarb.how: Cook the stalks with a little sweetener into compotes, crumbles or sauces. Only the stalks are eaten.
rhubarb.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
rhubarb.name: Rhubarb

olives.how: Eat as a snack, chop into salads and pasta, or blend into a tapenade; rinse if you want less brine.
olives.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
olives.reviewNote: Canned ripe olives show a lot of iron in the USDA record (6.3 mg per 100 g); that is partly iron added in processing, so the iron may not be representative of other olives. Very high in sodium (existing caution); sodium not shown.
olives.name: Olives

corn.desc: Corn, sweet, yellow, cooked, boiled, drained, without salt
corn.portion: 1 medium ear (USDA: 6¾–7½ in long = 103 g of kernels)
corn.how: Boil or steam an ear, cut the kernels into salads and soups, or grill the whole ear.
corn.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
corn.reviewNote: Sweet corn eaten as a vegetable; popcorn and cornmeal are separate foods.
corn.name: Corn

chicory.how: Use the bitter leaves raw in mixed salads, or wilt them in a pan with garlic.
chicory.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
chicory.reviewNote: The record is chicory greens; chicory root (as in coffee substitutes) is different.
chicory.name: Chicory

chive.how: Snip over eggs, potatoes, soups and dips just before serving.
chive.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
chive.name: Chive

dandelion.desc: Dandelion greens, cooked, boiled, drained, without salt
dandelion.portion: ½ cup chopped, cooked (USDA: 1 cup = 105 g)
dandelion.how: Sauté or simmer the greens; blanching first softens their bitterness.
dandelion.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
dandelion.name: Dandelion

endive.how: Use the crisp, slightly bitter leaves raw in salads, or braise or grill them.
endive.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
endive.reviewNote: USDA "endive" is curly endive; Belgian endive (witloof, a chicory) is a different vegetable.
endive.name: Endive

escarole.desc: Escarole, cooked, boiled, drained, no salt added
escarole.how: Wilt into soups and bean stews, sauté with garlic, or use the inner leaves raw.
escarole.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
escarole.reviewNote: USDA has only a cooked escarole record (escarole is commonly eaten raw too; raw would have more vitamin C).
escarole.name: Escarole

okra.desc: Okra, cooked, boiled, drained, without salt
okra.how: Sauté, roast, grill or add to stews; cooking whole or quickly keeps it less slippery.
okra.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
okra.name: Okra

scallion.desc: Onions, spring or scallions (includes tops and bulb), raw
scallion.how: Slice the white and green parts into stir-fries, noodles, eggs and dips, raw or cooked.
scallion.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
scallion.name: Scallion

daikon.how: Slice or grate raw into salads and pickles, or simmer in soups and braises.
daikon.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
daikon.name: Daikon

garlic.how: Crush or chop into sautés, dressings and soups; resting crushed garlic for a few minutes before cooking is a common kitchen habit.
garlic.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
garlic.name: Garlic

ginger.how: Grate or slice into stir-fries, soups, teas and marinades.
ginger.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
ginger.name: Ginger

leek.desc: Leeks, (bulb and lower leaf-portion), cooked, boiled, drained, without salt
leek.portion: ½ cup chopped, cooked (USDA: ¼ cup = 26 g)
leek.how: Wash well between the layers, slice, then sauté or simmer into soups, tarts and braises.
leek.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
leek.name: Leek

mustard-greens.desc: Mustard greens, cooked, boiled, drained, without salt
mustard-greens.portion: ½ cup chopped, cooked (USDA: 1 cup = 140 g)
mustard-greens.how: Sauté or simmer with garlic and a splash of acid; cooking softens their peppery bite.
mustard-greens.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
mustard-greens.name: Mustard greens

onion.how: Slice or chop raw into salads, or cook slowly until soft and sweet as a base for soups, stews and sauces.
onion.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
onion.name: Onion

watercress.how: Eat raw in salads and sandwiches, or stir into hot soup at the last minute.
watercress.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
watercress.name: Watercress

mint.how: Tear fresh leaves into salads, yoghurt sauces, fruit and drinks.
mint.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
mint.reviewNote: The catalogue has mint and peppermint separately; this is spearmint. The USDA record shows very high iron per 100 g (11.9 mg), but a normal use of mint is a few leaves, so the serving figures are small.
mint.name: Mint

peppermint.how: Use fresh leaves for tea or a garnish; the flavour is stronger than spearmint.
peppermint.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
peppermint.reviewNote: Peppermint tea or peppermint oil are different from the fresh leaf; a nutrient record does not cover any effect of them.
peppermint.name: Peppermint

canned-tomatoes.desc: Tomatoes, red, ripe, canned, packed in tomato juice
canned-tomatoes.how: Use as the base for soups, stews, sauces and braises; choose no-salt-added if you prefer to control salt.
canned-tomatoes.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
canned-tomatoes.reviewNote: This record is canned in juice with salt; a no-salt-added record also exists (170138).
canned-tomatoes.name: Canned tomatoes

celeriac.how: Peel, then roast, mash or simmer; or grate raw into slaws.
celeriac.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
celeriac.name: Celeriac

chili-pepper.how: Remove the seeds for less heat, and use sparingly in sauces, stir-fries, soups and salsas.
chili-pepper.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
chili-pepper.name: Chili pepper

fennel.how: Slice the bulb thin for salads, or roast or braise it until soft and sweet.
fennel.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
fennel.reviewNote: The bulb. Fennel seeds are a spice with different amounts.
fennel.name: Fennel

kohlrabi.how: Peel and eat raw in slaws, or roast, steam or add to soups.
kohlrabi.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
kohlrabi.name: Kohlrabi

plantain.how: Cook before eating: boil, bake or pan-fry slices; riper plantain is sweeter.
plantain.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
plantain.reviewNote: Plantain is normally cooked (fried, boiled, baked); frying adds fat. The record is raw yellow plantain; no cooked record was chosen.
plantain.name: Plantain

radicchio.how: Use raw in salads for a bitter note, or grill or roast wedges to soften it.
radicchio.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
radicchio.name: Radicchio

salsa.how: Serve with eggs, beans, tacos or grilled vegetables; check the label if you watch sodium.
salsa.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
salsa.reviewNote: A prepared food that varies by brand; high in sodium (no sourced caution added).
salsa.name: Salsa

shallot.how: Mince raw for dressings, or sauté gently as a milder alternative to onion.
shallot.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
shallot.name: Shallot

basil.how: Tear fresh leaves into salads, tomatoes and pasta, or blend into pesto; add to hot dishes at the end.
basil.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
basil.name: Basil

cilantro.how: Chop the leaves and tender stems into salsas, curries, rice and salads.
cilantro.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
cilantro.name: Cilantro (coriander)

dill.how: Use fresh sprigs with fish, potatoes, yoghurt sauces and pickles.
dill.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
dill.name: Dill

tomato-paste.desc: Tomato products, canned, paste, without salt added (Includes foods for USDA's Food Distribution Program)
tomato-paste.how: Fry a spoonful in oil at the start of a sauce or stew to deepen the flavour.
tomato-paste.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
tomato-paste.name: Tomato paste
